claim: Two macaque monkeys were trained to perform an urgent version of an oddball search task in which a red target appeared among three green distracters or vice versa.
source: To examine how selection history impacts saccadic choices, we trained two macaque monkeys to perform an urgent version of an oddball search task in which a red target appeared among three green distracters or vice versa.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental design and subjects used in the study.

claim: By imposing urgency, performance could be tracked continuously as it transitioned from uninformed guesses to informed choices as a function of processing time.
source: By imposing urgency, performance could be tracked continuously as it transitioned from uninformed guesses to informed choices as a function of processing time.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological approach and its capability to track performance transitions.

claim: The probability of making a correct choice was strongly modulated by the histories of preceding target locations and target colors.
source: Here, we found that the probability of making a correct choice was strongly modulated by the histories of preceding target locations and target colors.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Both location and color history effects were gated by success (or reward).
source: Crucially, although both effects were gated by success (or reward), their dynamics were clearly distinct
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that both effects depend on reward/success.

claim: Location history promoted a motor bias.
source: whereas location history promoted a motor bias, color history modulated perceptual sensitivity
evidence: This is a primary finding distinguishing the type of bias associated with location history.

claim: Color history modulated perceptual sensitivity.
source: whereas location history promoted a motor bias, color history modulated perceptual sensitivity
evidence: This is a primary finding distinguishing the type of bias associated with color history.

claim: Location and color history influences acted independently.
source: and these influences acted independently.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the independence of the two types of history effects.

claim: Combined selection histories can give rise to enormous swings in visuomotor performance even in simple tasks with highly discriminable stimuli.
source: Thus, combined selection histories can give rise to enormous swings in visuomotor performance even in simple tasks with highly discriminable stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Endogenous mechanisms allocate attention volitionally, prioritizing choices according to internal goals.
source: Endogenous mechanisms allocate attention volitionally, prioritizing choices according to internal goals, whereas exogenous mechanisms attract attention automatically in proportion to the physical saliencies of external features or events (Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 2010; Carrasco, 2011; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Exogenous mechanisms attract attention automatically in proportion to the physical saliencies of external features or events.
source: Endogenous mechanisms allocate attention volitionally, prioritizing choices according to internal goals, whereas exogenous mechanisms attract attention automatically in proportion to the physical saliencies of external features or events (Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 2010; Carrasco, 2011; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Current choices are constrained by the recent history of past choices in ways that are neither consistent with task goals nor a straightforward reflection of the physical saliencies of available options.
source: It is now generally accepted that current choices are constrained by the recent history of past choices in ways that are neither consistent with task goals nor a straightforward reflection of the physical saliencies of available options (Fecteau and Munoz, 2003; Awh et al., 2012; Theeuwes, 2018; Theeuwes, 2019; Anderson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Selection history is the umbrella term for attention mechanisms that comprise a collection of implicit biases shaped by past experience.
source: 'Selection history' is the umbrella term for attention mechanisms that are distinct from stimulus-driven and goal-directed forms in that they comprise a collection of implicit biases shaped by past experience.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided in the manuscript.

claim: Potential sources of selection history bias include feature-based priming, location bias, and stimulus- or action-reward associations.
source: Potential sources of selection history bias include feature-based priming (Maljkovic and Nakayama, 1994; McPeek et al., 1999; Kristjánsson and Campana, 2010; Brascamp et al., 2011; Kristjánsson and Ásgeirsson, 2019), location bias (Maljkovic and Nakayama, 1996; Chelazzi et al., 2014; Hickey et al., 2014), and stimulus- or action-reward associations (Barraclough et al., 2004; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Anderson et al., 2011; Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Hauser et al., 2018; Anderson, 2019; Hermoso-Mendizabal et al., 2020; Lak et al., 2020), among others.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: For PT < 100 ms, the performance of both monkey subjects was at chance (probability correct = 0.25), indicating that such choices were not informed by the color cue.
source: For PT < 100 ms, the performance of both monkey subjects was at chance (probability correct = 0.25), indicating that such choices were not informed by the color cue.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The measured ceiling levels seem unusually low for a visuomotor task in which the response rule is so simple and the stimuli so highly discriminable.
source: The measured ceiling levels seem unusually low for a visuomotor task in which the response rule is so simple and the stimuli so highly discriminable.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation made by the authors based on their data.

claim: The ceiling accuracies of the monkeys did not improve over the course of extensive training.
source: This is because, although our subjects practiced the CO task extensively (Figure 1b, caption) throughout several months of data collection, their ceiling accuracies did not improve (the Pearson correlation between experimental session and ceiling performance was 0.2, p=0.1 for monkey C and 0.05, p=0.6 for monkey N).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the training data showing no improvement over time.

claim: Other animals from the laboratory reached high ceilings (∼95% correct) in the urgent CO task when the target color remained fixed or when it switched only between blocks of trials.
source: This is because other animals from our laboratory reached high ceilings (∼95% correct) in the urgent CO task when the target color remained fixed or when it switched only between blocks of trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Scerra et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to data from a previous study by the same laboratory.

claim: What makes the CO task particularly difficult is the randomization of the target colors and locations.
source: Together, these two observations suggest that what makes the CO task particularly difficult is the randomization of the target colors and locations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing performance under different task conditions.

claim: Monkey performance was much lower when both color and location were randomized than when the target colors alternated between blocks of trials or between days.
source: Indeed, the same conclusion would be reached based on prior studies that used standard nonurgent versions of the oddball task; in that case, monkey performance was also much lower when both color and location were randomized (Song and McPeek, 2015) than when the target colors alternated between blocks of trials (Bichot and Schall, 1999; Bichot and Schall, 2002) or between days (McPeek and Keller, 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from multiple prior studies.

claim: The influence of target color repetition only became apparent at PT > 100 ms.
source: The influence of target color repetition only became apparent at PT > 100 ms, an inflection point that marks the transition from uninformed choices to those increasingly steered by color information.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Each additional preceding trial of the same target color was associated with a performance increment, as evident in both the slopes and ceiling values of the corresponding tachometric curves.
source: From there, each additional preceding trial of the same target color (1S–4S) was associated with a performance increment, as evident in both the slopes and ceiling values of the corresponding tachometric curves (Figure 2a, blue curves; Figure 2c, blue bars).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Color history had no measurable effect on uninformed choices, as indicated by uniformity of the floor accuracies across the range of history conditions.
source: Importantly, this perceptual bias altered the efficacy with which color information guided the choice, but, as expected, had no measurable effect on uninformed choices, as indicated by uniformity of the floor accuracies across the range of history conditions (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The principal effect of target location repetition was on uninformed choices (PT < 100 ms), those made before cue information began to guide behavior.
source: In contrast, the principal effect of target location repetition was on uninformed choices (Figure 2e and f), those made at PT < 100 ms, before cue information began to guide behavior.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For perceptually uninformed choices, or guesses, the likelihood of looking toward a given location increased as a function of the number of preceding trials in which the target appeared at that location.
source: For these perceptually uninformed choices, or guesses, the likelihood of looking toward a given location increased as a function of the number of preceding trials in which the target appeared at that location (Figure 2e, blue curves; Figure 2f, blue bars)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For location, the corresponding bias demonstrates the inverse trend: it is strongest for uninformed choices and decreases progressively after the inflection point.
source: In contrast, for location (black traces), the corresponding bias demonstrates the inverse trend: it is strongest for uninformed choices and decreases progressively after the inflection point.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis of difference curves in the data.

claim: For both color and location bias, the size of the computed differential trend increases monotonically as the number of S and D repetitions increases from one to four.
source: For both color and location bias, the size of the computed differential trend increases monotonically as the number of S and D repetitions increases from one (Figure 3a, 1S–1D) to four (Figure 3d, 4S–4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A single-color event had no impact on a future uninformed choice, as indicated by the floors of the tachometric curves obtained for different trial separations.
source: As anticipated, a single-color event, whether corresponding to a repeat or a switch, had no impact on a future uninformed choice, as indicated by the floors of the tachometric curves obtained for different trial separations (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Single-color events did impact future informed choices, as indicated by the ceilings of the tachometric curves.
source: However, single-color events did impact future informed choices, as indicated by the ceilings of the same curves (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The impact of a color repeat versus a switch accounted for a difference of approximately 13 percentage points in the likelihood of making a correct informed choice on the trial immediately following the reference event.
source: The impact of a color repeat (Figure 4b, S conditions, blue circles) versus a switch (Figure 4b, D conditions, brown circles) was fairly symmetric about a mean performance baseline and accounted for a difference of approximately 13 percentage points in the likelihood of making a correct informed choice on the trial immediately following the reference event (1S versus 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The color bias decayed within 5 trials or so; it had a demonstrable influence over informed choices for the next 4 trials but largely faded thereafter.
source: This color bias decayed within 5 trials or so; it had a demonstrable influence over informed choices for the next 4 trials (Figure 4b, 1S4x versus 1D4x; note separation between 95% CIs) but largely faded thereafter.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The time course of color bias is highly consistent with prior measurements based on nonurgent versions of the oddball task.
source: Such time course is highly consistent with prior measurements based on nonurgent versions of the oddball task (Bichot and Schall, 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from a prior study.

claim: The biasing effect of a location event produced a maximum difference of 7 percentage points in ceiling accuracy.
source: In this case, the biasing effect of a location event, whether a repeat (S conditions) or a switch (D conditions), was smaller overall, producing a maximum difference of 7 percentage points in ceiling accuracy (Figure 4, 1S versus 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The location bias was evident for both uninformed and informed choices and showed greater persistence than the color bias.
source: More importantly, the location bias was evident for both uninformed (Figure 4c, floor) and informed choices (Figure 4d, ceiling) and showed greater persistence than the color bias.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A single location event had a significant influence up to 9 trials into the future.
source: In this case, a single event had a significant influence up to 9 trials into the future (Figure 4c, d, 1S8x versus 1D8x; note separation between 95% CIs).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For tachometric curves in which each choice was preceded by four trials of the same target color, there was a difference of nearly 50 percentage points in ceiling performance depending on whether the previous same-color trials were correct or incorrect.
source: For example, for tachometric curves in which each choice was preceded by four trials of the same target color, we observed a difference of nearly 50 percentage points in ceiling performance depending on whether the previous same-color trials were correct or incorrect (Figure 5a, light green versus light magenta traces; Figure 5c, 4SC versus 4SE).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For repeats of the same target color, a history of successful outcomes increased the likelihood of correctly choosing the target, whereas a history of unsuccessful outcomes decreased this likelihood.
source: Thus, for repeats of the same target color, a history of successful outcomes increased the likelihood of correctly choosing the target, whereas a history of unsuccessful outcomes decreased this likelihood.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: When the same target location was repeated, the outcome either reinforced or diminished the likelihood of choosing the target, depending on whether the repeats were associated with correct or incorrect choices.
source: When the same target location was repeated, the outcome either reinforced or diminished the likelihood of choosing the target, depending on whether the repeats were associated with correct (Figure 6a–c, green) or incorrect (Figure 6a–c, magenta) choices.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Outcome-dependent variations in motor bias were most evident for uninformed choices, as indicated by modulation of the floor values of the conditioned tachometric curves.
source: As expected, these outcome-dependent variations in motor bias were most evident for uninformed choices, as indicated by modulation of the floor values (Figure 6b and f) of the conditioned tachometric curves (Figure 6a and e).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The effects of unrewarded (error) outcomes on accuracy are consistent with the idea that these expressions of bias were not the product of a deliberate strategy to optimize behavior.
source: The effects of unrewarded (error) outcomes on accuracy are consistent with the idea that these expressions of bias were not the product of a deliberate strategy to optimize behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The attribution of outcome on each trial was to the color of the singleton, not the color of the distracter that was erroneously targeted by the saccade.
source: This, in turn, suggests that the attribution of outcome on each trial was to the color of the singleton (e.g., red), not the color of the distracter (e.g., green) that was erroneously targeted by the saccade – an attribution that ignores the role of the motor act in causing the outcome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: RTs tended to be shorter when preceded by one or more error trials and longer when preceded by correct trials.
source: Specifically, RTs tended to be shorter when preceded by one or more error trials (Figures 5d, h, 6d and h, magenta) and longer when preceded by correct trials (Figures 5d, h, 6d and h, green).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The data generally lie along the diagonal with regression slopes close to 1, indicating that color and location histories influence ceiling performance independently of each other.
source: But critically, the pattern that emerges is similar for all the history lengths: the data generally lie along the diagonal, with regression slopes close to 1 (Figure 7a, blue lines and β2 coefficients). This indicates that, to a first approximation, color and location histories influence ceiling performance independently of each other.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the statistical analysis shown in figures.

claim: For color and outcome histories, the results of the independence analysis are consistent with an underlying functional interaction.
source: Thus, as expected, for color and outcome histories, the results of this independence analysis are consistent with an underlying functional interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: The discrepancies between predicted and measured probabilities were slightly larger for location and outcome than for color and outcome.
source: Very similar results were obtained when we considered the combined effect of target location and outcome histories, except that the discrepancies between predicted and measured probabilities were slightly larger than for color and outcome (Figure 7c, blue lines and β2 coefficients).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the statistical analysis shown in figures.

claim: The data show that color- and location-driven biases exert largely independent effects on ceiling performance, especially once outcome history is taken into consideration.
source: The data show that color- and location-driven biases exert largely independent effects on ceiling performance, especially once outcome history is taken into consideration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: The results from analyses based on predictability are consistent with the notion that although both color and location histories interact strongly with outcome history, the resulting color- and location-driven biases make approximately independent contributions to performance during informed choices.
source: In summary, the results from our analyses based on predictability are consistent with the notion that although both color and location histories interact strongly with outcome history, the resulting color- and location-driven biases make approximately independent contributions to performance during informed choices.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the statistical analyses.

claim: While RTs tended to be somewhat idiosyncratic, variations in choice accuracy across history conditions were highly consistent in both sign and magnitude across the two monkey subjects.
source: Interestingly, though, we found that while RTs indeed tended to be somewhat idiosyncratic, variations in choice accuracy across history conditions were highly consistent in both sign and magnitude across the two monkey subjects.
evidence: This is a direct observation from comparing data across the two subjects.

claim: During uninformed choices, color history had essentially no impact, whereas saccades were strongly biased toward prior target locations, especially when they were associated with success (or reward).
source: During uninformed choices (Figure 8a), color history had essentially no impact, whereas saccades were strongly biased toward prior target locations, especially when they were associated with success (or reward).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Across subjects, the modulations of the floor of the tachometric curve were nearly identical.
source: Across subjects, the corresponding modulations of the floor of the tachometric curve were nearly identical.
evidence: This is a direct observation from comparing data across the two subjects.

claim: During informed choices, the effect of location history alone was more subtle than that of color alone, but both dimensions had a remarkably strong impact on performance when prior outcomes were taken into account.
source: During informed choices (Figure 8b), the effect of location history alone was more subtle than that of color alone, but both dimensions had a remarkably strong impact on performance when prior outcomes were taken into account.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Monkey N generally responded more slowly than monkey C.
source: First, as noted earlier, monkey N generally responded more slowly (Figure 1d). This was visible in the data (Figure 8c, note difference between dotted lines) even after having downshifted all the RTs of this subject (by 29 ms; Methods).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The magnitudes of the history-driven modulations in RT were considerably larger for monkey N than for monkey C when trial outcome was taken into account.
source: And second, the magnitudes of the history-driven modulations in RT were considerably larger for monkey N than for monkey C when trial outcome was taken into account (Figure 8c, histories conditioned on outcome).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The tachometric curve is minimally sensitive to variations in urgency or motor preparation.
source: They also illustrate a key property of the tachometric curve, which is that it is minimally sensitive to variations in urgency or motor preparation (Stanford et al., 2010; Shankar et al., 2011; Seideman et al., 2018; Stanford and Salinas, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: When trials are parsed according to PT, the variability in performance due to urgency is drastically curtailed.
source: This is because, when trials are parsed according to PT, the variability in performance due to urgency is drastically curtailed.
evidence: This is an explanation of a methodological property based on prior work.

claim: Derived measures of choice accuracy, including the floor and ceiling values, are largely indicative of sensory and cognitive processing but not motor processing.
source: As a consequence, derived measures of choice accuracy, including the floor and ceiling values, are largely indicative of sensory and cognitive processing but not motor processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the methodological approach.

claim: A large lapse rate (∼35%) that could be naively interpreted as stochastic behavior due to internal noise sources turned out to correspond to the manifestation of short-term biases driven by the recent history of events preceding each choice.
source: As in prior studies (Busse et al., 2011; Gupta et al., 2024), a large lapse rate (∼35% in our case) that could be naively interpreted as stochastic behavior due to internal noise sources turned out to correspond, instead, to the manifestation of short-term biases driven by the recent history of events preceding each choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of prior studies.

claim: The histories associated with target location and target color made large contributions to choice accuracy that were associated with motor and perceptual mechanisms, respectively.
source: With this approach, we found that the histories associated with target location and target color made large contributions to choice accuracy that (1) were associated with motor and perceptual mechanisms, respectively
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Location and color history effects had distinct time constants.
source: (2) had distinct time constants
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Both location and color history effects depended strongly on the success of past trials.
source: (3) in both cases depended strongly on the success of past trials
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Location and color history effects acted independently of each other during perceptually informed trials to a large degree.
source: (4) to a large degree acted independently of each other during perceptually informed trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The motor bias observed is highly consistent with experiments showing that monkeys make much faster and much more accurate saccades to spatial locations that have been recently associated with a large reward than to locations that have not.
source: On one hand, the motor bias we observed is highly consistent with experiments showing that monkeys make much faster and much more accurate saccades to spatial locations that have been recently associated with a large reward than to locations that have not (Lauwereyns et al., 2002; Ikeda and Hikosaka, 2003; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Isoda and Hikosaka, 2008; Hauser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from multiple prior studies.

claim: Such reward-driven spatial effects are caused by the recent history of reward-driven reinforcement going back a few (1–15) trials.
source: Such effects are caused by the recent history of reward-driven reinforcement going back a few (1–15) trials
evidence: This is a characterization based on prior literature.

claim: Expression of the strong bias in favor of previously rewarded target locations is likely to depend on the urgent nature of the CO task.
source: Interestingly, however, expression of the strong bias that we observed in favor of previously rewarded target locations is likely to depend on the urgent nature of the CO task, because under nonurgent but otherwise comparable conditions, target location repetitions had no discernible effect on accuracy and only a small influence on RT (Bichot and Schall, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing the current findings to prior work.

claim: The perceptual bias observed is highly consistent with color priming, a well-known effect whereby the perceptual processing of a given color in one trial facilitates the processing of the same color in the next trial.
source: On the other hand, the perceptual bias we observed is highly consistent with color priming, a well-known effect whereby the perceptual processing of a given color in one trial facilitates the processing of the same color in the next trial.
evidence: This is a comparison to a well-established phenomenon in the literature.

claim: The color bias in the CO task is most likely the same as the 'priming of pop-out' reported in human participants.
source: Although priming effects are typically reported as differences in RT, the color bias in the CO task is most likely the same as the 'priming of pop-out' reported in human participants (Maljkovic and Nakayama, 1994; McPeek et al., 1999)
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from prior studies in humans.

claim: Priming of pop-out is characterized as an attention-focusing mechanism that builds up cumulatively, decays within 5–8 trials, and is largely involuntary.
source: which is characterized as an attention-focusing mechanism that builds up cumulatively (as in Figures 2a–d–3), decays within 5–8 trials (as in Figure 4b), and is largely involuntary (consistent with permanence in spite of months of practice).
evidence: This is a characterization based on prior literature and consistency with current findings.

claim: The priming results can be explained by short-lived adaptation in the responses of identified neural circuits in visual and oculomotor areas, which convey information about object salience and thereby guide the selection of saccade targets.
source: As with the motor bias, neurophysiological studies again indicate that the phenomenology is entirely compatible with known attention mechanisms; i.e., the priming results can be explained by short-lived adaptation in the responses of identified neural circuits in visual and oculomotor areas, which convey information about object salience and thereby guide the selection of saccade targets (Westerberg and Schall, 2021).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on prior neurophysiological studies.

claim: The color priming effect seems to be minimally affected by urgency.
source: In contrast to the motor bias, the color priming effect seems to be minimally affected by urgency, because its impact on choice accuracy under nonurgent conditions (Bichot and Schall, 2002) was comparable to that found here.
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from a prior study.

claim: The qualitative similarity between spatial and feature-based selection history effects as found in the CO task and in simpler, nonurgent tasks suggests that these effects are highly robust and relevant to real-world situations.
source: Two observations suggest that spatial and feature-based selection history effects are highly robust and hence relevant to real-world situations. First, the qualitative similarity just discussed between such effects as found in the CO task and in simpler, nonurgent tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing findings across different task conditions.

claim: Spatial and feature-based selection history effects are not strategic, on average neither helping nor hindering overall performance.
source: And second, the fact that they are not strategic, on average neither helping nor hindering overall performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A study that directly compared serial dependencies and color priming found that their effects were uncorrelated and concluded that they are mediated by separate mechanisms.
source: Indeed, a study that directly compared them found that their effects were uncorrelated and concluded that they are mediated by separate mechanisms (Galluzzi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a reference to findings from a prior study.

claim: The contribution of recent history to behavioral variability is likely much larger than is generally appreciated, particularly under more naturalistic, less constrained conditions during which multiple such effects may be expressed.
source: Given this, and the remarkable degree to which the performance of our monkey subjects was swayed by history-driven biases, we conclude that the contribution of recent history to behavioral variability is likely much larger than is generally appreciated, particularly under more naturalistic, less constrained conditions during which multiple such effects may be expressed (Kattner et al., 2025).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their implications.

claim: Data were obtained from two purpose-bred adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, 7 years of age).
source: Data were obtained from two purpose-bred adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, 7 years of age)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: For monkey C, data were collected in the span of 20 months, in 79 experimental sessions that yielded 26,038 trials of the CO task.
source: For monkey C, data were collected in the span of 20 months, in 79 experimental sessions that yielded 26,038 trials of the CO task.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection for one subject.

claim: For monkey N, data were collected in the span of 21 months, in 105 experimental sessions that yielded 45,173 trials.
source: For monkey N, data were collected in the span of 21 months, in 105 experimental sessions that yielded 45,173 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection for one subject.

claim: The CO task is an urgent four-alternative choice paradigm in which subjects must make a saccade to a color singleton presented among three uniformly colored distracters.
source: The CO task (Figure 1a) is an urgent four-alternative choice paradigm in which subjects must make a saccade to a color singleton presented among three uniformly colored distracters (Scerra et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: Target identities and locations are randomly and independently assigned from trial to trial such that the prior probability of a color repetition is 0.5, and the prior probability of a location repetition is 0.25.
source: Target identities and locations are randomly and independently assigned from trial to trial such that the prior probability of a color repetition is 0.5, and the prior probability of a location repetition is 0.25.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Before pooling the data from the two monkeys, 29 ms was subtracted from all the RTs from monkey N, which in turn shifted all its PTs by the same amount.
source: Thus, before pooling the data from the two monkeys, we first subtracted 29 ms from all the RTs from monkey N, which in turn shifted all its PTs by the same amount.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.
